q: Which of the following best defines money?
options: Anything widely accepted in exchange for goods and services
Only notes issued by the central bank
explain: Money is defined by general acceptance as a medium of exchange, not by its material or by who issues it.

q: Which of the following is an example of commodity money?
explain: Commodity money has intrinsic value outside its use as money; salt, gold, silver, copper and rice are examples.

q: Fiat money has value because
options: it can always be exchanged for gold
the government has decreed that it has value as money
it is made of precious metal
explain: Fiat money has no intrinsic value and no convertibility into a commodity; its value rests on government decree.

q: Currency notes and coins are called fiat money because
options: they are made on special imported paper
they are printed by the government
they exchange for goods and services
they do not have intrinsic value like gold or silver
explain: Many things exchange for goods and are printed by governments; the defining feature of fiat money is the lack of intrinsic value.

q: Token coins and certificates that can be exchanged for a commodity are an example of
explain: Representative money stands for a commodity and is exchangeable for it; the commodity itself is commodity money.

q: The right of minting coins is the monopoly of
explain: Metallic money is minted only under the authority of the government.

q: Bonds and government debentures are treated as which type of money?
explain: They are not exact money but are close to it because they are highly liquid, hence adjacent money.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of digital money?
explain: Digital money exists purely in electronic form; metallic coins are physical.

q: Which statement about digital money is correct?
options: It is susceptible to hacks and can compromise user privacy
It is physically tangible like a banknote
It cannot be used by central banks
It makes transactions slower and costlier
explain: Digital money can make payments cheaper and faster, but it carries hacking and privacy risks.

q: Which of the following makes up reserve money (M0)?
options: Currency with the public + demand deposits with banks
Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with the RBI + 'other' deposits with the RBI
explain: M0 is the RBI's monetary base: currency in circulation plus bankers' and other deposits with the RBI.

q: M1 consists of
options: currency with the public + time deposits with banks
currency with the public + demand deposits with the banking system + 'other' deposits with the RBI
explain: M1 is the narrow measure: cash with the public plus demand-type deposits.

q: M2 is equal to
options: M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks
explain: M2 adds post office savings bank deposits to M1; time deposits enter only in M3.

q: M3 is calculated as
options: M1 + time deposits with the banking system
M1 + savings deposits with post offices
explain: M3 = M1 plus time deposits with banks; it is the broad concept of money supply.

q: In the money supply classification, M4 equals
options: M3 + all deposits with post office savings banks (excluding National Savings Certificates)
M1 + demand deposits with the RBI
explain: M4 widens M3 with all post office savings deposits, but NSCs are excluded.

q: In India, which of the following is called 'broad money'?
explain: M3 is the broad money concept; banks base their lending programmes on it since it lies with them for a known period.

q: Why is M1 called narrow money?
options: It is the smallest component of M0
It is held only by the RBI
It is highly liquid, so banks cannot run their lending programmes on it
explain: M1 is mostly cash and demand deposits that can be withdrawn at any time, so banks cannot lend it out for fixed periods.

q: As we move from M1 to M4, the liquidity of money
explain: Each wider measure adds less liquid deposits, so liquidity falls from M1 to M4.

q: Which of the following money supply measures includes time deposits with banks but NOT post office deposits?
explain: M3 adds time deposits to M1; post office deposits appear in M2 (savings) and M4 (all).

q: The note-issue system followed in India is the
explain: Since the system adopted in 1957 the RBI keeps a fixed minimum reserve of gold and foreign securities and may issue notes of any amount.

q: Under the Minimum Reserve System, the RBI's minimum reserve in gold and foreign securities is
options: ₹115 crore, of which ₹200 crore is gold
₹200 crore, of which at least ₹115 crore is gold
explain: The reserve totals ₹200 crore, with gold and gold coin at least ₹115 crore; foreign securities make up the remainder.

q: Who is the final authority for deciding the design, form and material of bank notes in India?
explain: The RBI recommends, but the Central Government has the final say on design, form and material of notes.

q: Who decides the quantity of coins to be minted in India?
explain: Coin minting is a government function, so the quantity is decided by the Government of India.

q: When someone buys foreign currency against rupees, the banks provide the equivalent amount based on the prevailing
explain: The price of one currency in terms of another is the exchange rate.

q: On 25 September 1975 the rupee was delinked from pound sterling and linked to
explain: From 1975 the rupee's value was determined with reference to a basket of currencies.

q: Under the Bretton Woods System, India as an IMF member declared the par value of the rupee in terms of
explain: India declared the par value of the rupee in terms of gold as an IMF member under the Bretton Woods system.

q: The ₹500 note was re-introduced in India in
explain: The RBI began note production in 1938; the ₹500 note was re-introduced in 1987.

q: The rupee's association with pound sterling as the intervention currency was broken in
explain: The sterling link as intervention currency ended in 1992.

q: Which statement about the money market is correct?
options: It deals in long-term equity and debt claims
It deals only in foreign currency
It is a short-term credit market regulated by the Reserve Bank of India
explain: The money market is where short-term funds are borrowed and lent, under RBI regulation.

q: Which of the following is NOT a money market instrument?
explain: Equity shares are long-term capital market instruments.

q: Which market deals in long-term debt and equity claims?
explain: The money market handles short-term funds; the capital market handles long-term debt and equity.

q: Which of the following are lenders in the money market?
options: Commercial banks, insurance companies, finance companies and the central bank
explain: Money market lenders include banks, insurers, finance companies and the central bank.

q: Treasury bills are issued by
options: the Government of India through auctions
explain: State Governments do not issue treasury bills; the Government of India does, through auctions.

q: Treasury bills are issued at
options: a discount and redeemed at par
par and redeemed at a premium
a premium and redeemed at par
par and redeemed at a discount
explain: T-bills are zero-coupon: bought below face value and repaid at face value.

q: The minimum amount for which treasury bills are available is
explain: T-bills are available for a minimum of ₹25,000 and in multiples of ₹25,000.

q: The central government issued treasury bills to fulfil which requirement of banks?
explain: Treasury bills are government securities that count towards banks' Statutory Liquidity Ratio.

q: What is the generally maximum maturity of a treasury bill?
explain: T-bills are short-term securities for up to one year (364 days).

q: Commercial paper in India was introduced in
explain: CP was introduced in 1990 so that highly rated corporates could diversify short-term borrowing; CDs date to 1989.

q: Commercial paper can be issued in denominations of
explain: The minimum CP denomination is ₹5 lakh; for CDs it is ₹1 lakh.

q: The minimum amount of a certificate of deposit is
explain: A CD must be at least ₹1 lakh and in multiples of ₹1 lakh thereafter.

q: A company issuing commercial paper must have a tangible net worth of at least
explain: One of the CP eligibility conditions is tangible net worth of not less than ₹4 crore.

q: The minimum credit rating required for issuing commercial paper is
explain: The issuer must have a rating of at least A-2 as per SEBI's rating symbols.

q: Commercial paper can be issued for a maturity between
explain: CP maturity runs from 7 days to one year, but not beyond the validity of the issuer's rating.

q: For which maturity can financial institutions issue certificates of deposit?
options: More than 1 year and up to 3 years
explain: Banks issue CDs for 7 days to 1 year; FIs issue them for 1 to 3 years.

q: Which statement about commercial paper is correct?
options: It is issued only by commercial banks
It is secured against the issuer's assets
It can be issued only by the government
It is an unsecured instrument issued in the form of a promissory note
explain: CP is unsecured; it is issued by highly rated corporates, primary dealers and all-India FIs.

q: Which of the following cannot issue certificates of deposit?
options: Select all-India financial institutions permitted by RBI
explain: CDs may be issued by scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs and Local Area Banks) and permitted FIs.

q: 'Call money' refers to funds that are borrowed and lent
explain: Call money is overnight; notice money covers 2 to 14 days and term money 15 days to 1 year.

q: Notice money in the money market means funds borrowed for
explain: Notice money covers 2 to 14 days.

q: Term money refers to deals in funds for
explain: Term money covers the span from 15 days up to a year.

q: In a repurchase agreement (repo), the repurchase price compared with the original sale price is
options: lower, the difference being a discount
explain: The seller buys back at a higher price; the difference is effectively interest (the repo rate).

q: A banker's acceptance is
options: an unsecured note issued by a corporate
a short-term credit instrument guaranteed by a bank and used extensively in foreign trade
a deposit certificate of a financial institution
explain: BAs are created by a non-financial firm, guaranteed by a bank, traded at a discount and considered very safe.

q: Which of the following can participate in the call and notice money market both as borrowers and lenders?
options: Only the RBI and the government
Scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs), co-operative banks (other than Land Development Banks) and primary dealers
Regional Rural Banks and Land Development Banks
explain: RRBs and Land Development Banks are excluded; PDs, co-operative banks and scheduled commercial banks take part.

q: CBLO was operated by the
explain: CCIL ran CBLO for entities without access, or with restricted access, to the call money market. It was discontinued in November 2018.

q: Organised chit funds in India are regulated by the
options: Registrar of Chit Funds under the Chit Funds Act, 1982
RBI under the Banking Regulation Act
explain: Chit funds are governed by the Chit Funds Act, 1982 and supervised by the Registrar of Chit Funds.

q: Which of the following belongs to the unorganised money market?
explain: The unorganised market consists of unregulated non-bank intermediaries such as moneylenders, chit funds and nidhis.

q: Stagflation implies
explain: Stagflation combines stagnant output (recession) with rising prices.

q: Cheap money implies
explain: Cheap money means credit is available at low interest rates.

q: Deficit financing aims at economic development, but if it fails it generates
explain: Printing extra currency to fill the gap between expenditure and revenue raises the money supply and prices.

q: A steady increase in the general price level because aggregate demand grows faster than aggregate supply is called
explain: Demand-pull inflation arises when demand outruns supply; cost-push arises from rising input costs.

q: If banks and the private sector decide to hold less cash, the money multiplier will be
explain: Less cash held means more of each deposit is re-lent, so the multiplier rises.

q: The rate of inflation increases when the purchasing power of money
explain: Inflation is a fall in the purchasing power of money.

q: What is MZM in the money market?
explain: MZM stands for money of zero maturity, i.e. money that can be spent immediately.
